title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing, Founder University and media: bet on "what if it works"
summary: Jason explains how he invests (high-volume small checks, "what if it works"), how Launch and Founder University filter thousands of applicants, and how he approaches new media formats and interviewing. He also covers the Uber/Robinhood bets, Elon's work ethic, the Twitter overstaffing lesson and AI-driven job displacement.

principles.text: Judge new bets by asking 'what if it works?' instead of sizing the TAM; manifest the market.
principles.quote: I just said to myself, what if it works? Which is what I always say to myself. What if it works?

principles.text: Treat new media formats as a sandbox: assume they'll work, play early, and don't dwell on failures.
principles.quote: I've always looked at like new mediums coming out as like a playground, and I just assume they're going to work, and if they don't work, who cares?

principles.text: Early-stage investing is a volume game: many small checks across lots of surface area, since most seed companies go to zero.
principles.quote: You have to have a lot of bets and you don't know which one's going to hit.

principles.text: Founders should expect rejection as a numbers game: talk to hundreds of investors, since you only need a few yeses.
principles.quote: You don't need a hundred out of a hundred people to invest in your company. You need three out of a hundred, two out of a hundred

principles.text: Great interviews come from listening: the next best question is embedded in the previous answer, not on your list.
principles.quote: the next best question is embedded in the previous answer.

principles.text: Reduce rejection friction by repeating back a founder's vision before deciding; it raised satisfaction scores markedly.
principles.quote: can I repeat back your vision to you so I make sure I didn't miss anything and once we started doing that the ratings got much better
